HTTP/2 fixed **HTTP-layer** head-of-line (HOL) blocking, but it could not eliminate **transport-layer** HOL blocking because every multiplexed HTTP/2 stream shares one ordered TCP byte stream. HTTP/3 moves HTTP onto QUIC, whose transport-level streams are independently ordered—so a lost packet normally stalls only the affected stream(s), while unrelated streams can continue.[1][2]

## What HTTP/2 changed

HTTP/1.1 commonly suffered application-level HOL blocking: when requests were pipelined on one connection, a later response could be held up behind an earlier slow response.

HTTP/2 addressed that at the HTTP layer by splitting requests and responses into frames and multiplexing frames from many logical streams over one TCP connection. A slow response on stream A no longer inherently prevents the server from interleaving and sending data for stream B.[1][3]

But HTTP/2 still runs over TCP. TCP delivers one **strictly in-order sequence of bytes** to the application. If a TCP segment is lost, TCP withholds all later received bytes until it recovers the missing segment—even if those later bytes encode frames belonging to totally unrelated HTTP/2 streams. Thus, a loss event can temporarily stall every HTTP/2 request sharing that connection.[1][4]

## What HTTP/3 changed

HTTP/3 uses HTTP semantics over QUIC rather than TCP. QUIC runs over UDP but provides its own reliable delivery, encryption, congestion control, and—most important here—**native, independently ordered streams**.[2][4]

QUIC tracks data offsets per stream rather than requiring one connection-wide ordered byte sequence. Therefore:

| Situation | HTTP/2 over TCP | HTTP/3 over QUIC |
|---|---|---|
| A packet carrying data for one request is lost | TCP waits for the missing bytes before delivering later bytes from the connection; all HTTP/2 streams can be delayed | Only the QUIC stream(s) with missing data wait for recovery |
| Data for unrelated requests has already arrived | May remain inaccessible behind the TCP gap | Can be delivered immediately if complete for its own stream |
| Multiplexing layer | HTTP streams exist above TCP | QUIC transport supplies the independent streams that HTTP/3 uses |
| Result under packet loss | Connection-wide transport HOL blocking | No cross-stream transport HOL blocking |

This is the key architectural shift: HTTP/2 multiplexed at the **application protocol** layer, where TCP could not recognize stream boundaries. HTTP/3 relies on QUIC multiplexing at the **transport** layer, where loss recovery knows which stream’s data is missing.[1][4]

## Important limitation

“HTTP/3 eliminates HOL blocking” is useful shorthand, but not literally absolute. It eliminates **cross-stream transport HOL blocking**. Each individual QUIC stream still provides ordered, reliable delivery: if byte range 0–999 of a particular response is missing, later bytes on that *same* stream cannot be delivered to HTTP until the gap is repaired. The benefit is isolation—other streams remain able to progress.[5]

For example, imagine a page loading HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images concurrently:

- In HTTP/2, one lost TCP segment can pause delivery for every resource on that TCP connection.
- In HTTP/3, if the missing packet held part of an image response, that image’s stream may pause, but ready CSS or JavaScript data in other QUIC streams can still reach the browser.

The gain is especially meaningful on lossy or variable networks, such as mobile, Wi‑Fi, or congested links; on a clean, low-loss connection, the HOL-specific advantage may be much less visible.

- IETF’s [HTTP/3 specification (RFC 9114)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114) explains that HTTP/3 is mapped onto QUIC and discusses its stream behavior.[2]
- MDN’s [head-of-line blocking glossary](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Head_of_line_blocking) provides a concise explanation of the HTTP/2-versus-HTTP/3 distinction.[1]
- APNIC’s [technical walkthrough of HTTP/3 prioritization and HOL blocking](https://blog.apnic.net/2022/11/30/http-3-and-quic-prioritization-and-head-of-line-blocking/) usefully illustrates why TCP’s lack of stream awareness creates the HTTP/2 problem.[4]
